summary: Discovery call focused on sizing dedicated reserved GPU pools for Heterodyne Labs' production inference. Key concerns: predictable p95 latency under burst traffic, tenant isolation for multi-tenant workloads, encryption/KMS requirements, and cost tradeoffs between larger reserved pools vs. elastic burst. Agreement to run a short benchmark with a replay of peak traffic and to share pricing and sizing guidance.
transcript:
Meeting header: 2027-05-04 11:00 PT / 15:00 UTC, duration 58m. Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Luis Ortega (Redwood SE), Casey Novak (Redwood Solutions), Priya Raman (CTO - Heterodyne Labs), Jonas Fisk (Infra), Selena Ruiz (SecOps), Tom Becker (Product).

[00:00] Maya (Redwood): Hey everyone, thanks for joining. We'll do a quick intros round and then dig into your reserved capacity and burst needs.
[00:18] Priya (Heterodyne): Hi, yeah thanks. I'm Priya, CTO. Quick context: we're ramping from a research prototype to prod for our streaming summarization feature. We expect steady traffic, but have irregular spikes from scheduled reports and a couple of customers that can burst.
[00:33] Jonas (Heterodyne): Jonas here, infra. Main thing for us is isolation — we run multiple tenants and don't want noisy neighbor issues. Also cost predictability: procurement wants a clear monthly commit or else we go with CloudGiantAI.
[00:48] Luis (Redwood SE): Got it. When you say spikes, what's the amplitude and typical duration? Percentage over baseline?
[00:56] Priya: Baseline is ~250 requests/min, spikes to ~1,800-2,200 RPM for 5-20 minutes during report windows. Token counts vary — average 200 tokens, occasional 1k token jobs.
[01:18] Tom (Product): We have a couple of latency-sensitive routes (realtime chat) that need p95 < 450ms. Non-critical batch jobs can be best-effort.
[01:31] Casey (Redwood): Good, that split helps. For dedicated we usually advise a warm-pool/reserved ratio so your critical routes hit reserved capacity with prewarmed KV cache and the rest land on hosted or burst nodes.
[01:46] Selena (Heterodyne): A couple security questions up front: do you support customer-managed KMS/HSM with Private? We need separation of keys, also SAML SSO and RBAC for operator accounts.
[02:02] Maya: Yes — Redwood Private supports KMS integrations and HSM-backed keys, SAML SSO and fine-grained RBAC. We'll share our security pack.
[02:10] Selena: And SOC2, audit logs?
[02:12] Maya: SOC2 Type II available for enterprise customers and we have audit logs and traceability per request-token level in the Console.
[02:20] [00:02:20] Speaker 6: (mumble) sorry just joining.

[00:02:40] Luis: Back to sizing — two knobs: committed reserved GPUs (monthly/annual commit) and a warm-pool for prewarmed instances. The warm-pool is what reduces cold start and warms the KV cache for chat-like workloads.
[03:05] Jonas: For warm-pool, how quickly can you scale when a spike hits? Is warm-pool instantaneous or does it take minutes to spin up additional reserved nodes?
[03:15] Luis: Warm-pool nodes are kept prewarmed so p95 is stable. If you need additional capacity beyond the warm-pool, autoscaling from reserved can take 30-90s depending on model size and startup path. We also offer burst guards — policy-based routing to fall back to hosted compatible model variants when dedicated is at capacity.
[03:37] Priya: That fallback worries us — can fallback leak data to shared tenancy? We have strict data residency for some customers.
[03:45] Maya: Good flag. Fallback to hosted uses sanitized model variants and we can configure policies to disallow fallback for certain tenants. For regulated customers we'd recommend Private or Dedicated with strict routing, and we can enforce no-hosted-fallback in the policy.

[00:04:20] Tom: What about preemption? If a reserved pool is busy and you failover, what order do requests get evicted?
[04:35] Luis: We avoid preemption within a reserved pool. Preemption typically applies when using lower-tier shared capacity. For reserved pools, we surface queueing/backpressure and optional prioritization tokens so you can keep latency-critical routes prioritized.
[04:50] Priya: We need guaranteed throughput for our realtime customers. Can we do dedicated GPUs per tenant?
[04:58] Casey: You can carve tenant-level isolation in the reserved pool with node affinity and tenant fencing. There is an ops tradeoff — more strict isolation means lower packing efficiency and higher cost. We can show pre-warm/topology options.

[00:05:20] Selena: Encryption at rest and in transit — we need TLS + mTLS for service-to-service, and disk encryption keys under our KMS. Any roadblocks to on-prem private deployment?
[05:35] Luis: For on-prem we provide a Private control plane and customer-managed networking. HSM integration is supported in our Private package. The work there is typically network and audit pipeline integration.
[05:47] Selena: Ok. Also curious about model versions and rollouts: if we upgrade a model, can we canary to a subset of reserved nodes?
[05:57] Maya: Yes — Redwood supports model rollouts by percent and canary to specific pools, with automatic fallback if quality regressions trigger.

[00:06:20] Jonas: Let's talk numbers — If baseline is 250 RPM with 200 tokens avg and spikes to 2,000 RPM, what's a starting reserved GPU count?
[06:38] Luis: Rough calc: tokens per second baseline roughly (250 req/min * 200 tokens) = ~833 tokens/sec baseline; spike ~ (2000/60 * 200) = ~6,667 tokens/sec. Model throughput depends on model and quantization. If you run a mid-sized Llama variant at int8 on A100-style nodes, single GPU sustained might do ~120-200 tokens/sec for generation workloads. So for the spike you'd need many GPUs. Practically we size by latency SLO: pick GPUs to keep p95 under 450ms for critical routes. We'll run the replay to get precise numbers.
[07:14] Priya: Ok that's rough but helpful. Could be dozens of GPUs if we need low-latency for long outputs. Cost becomes big.
[07:22] Maya: Which is why customers mix reserved for critical routes and use dynamic burst (hosted) for large intermittent traffic. Reserved buys predictability for the small, high-SLO slice.

[00:07:40] Tom: Can you do a hybrid where the host fallback uses a quantized variant that is cheaper but similar quality?
[07:52] Luis: Absolutely — policy can route overflow to a compatible, quantized variant. We also have recommendations in Redwood Optimize for quantization and batch sizes that minimize quality regression.

[00:08:10] Priya: Compliance question: we have EU customers; data residency matters. Can dedicated be provisioned in EU region and is Private available for on-prem EU?
[08:25] Maya: Yes to both. We operate in multiple regions and Private can be deployed into EU on-prem stacks. We'll note EU region for the proposal.

[00:08:45] Jonas: How does KV cache warming work across nodes? If traffic hits different nodes, do you get cache misses and token regen latency?
[08:58] Luis: KV cache is per-inference process; for chat workloads we typically steer sticky sessions to warmed nodes within the reserved pool. For very bursty distributed traffic there will be some cache churn. Warm-pool and session affinity reduce misses.
[09:15] Selena: Is session affinity sticky by token or by user id?
[09:18] Casey: You can use either. We support header-based affinity and token-aware routing.

[00:09:40] Priya: For procurement — what contract lengths and commit discounts do you offer? We need both monthly and annual options.
[09:55] Maya: We have monthly, 12-month, and 36-month reserved tiers. Typical discounts scale with commit size and term. We'll include a pricing matrix and an example SLO-backed commitment.
[10:08] Tom: Do you charge for warm-pool nodes separately?
[10:12] Maya: Warm-pool is priced as part of reserved capacity; short prewarmed bursts can be included as burst credits on top of commit, or you can pay for larger committed pool to avoid any burst billing. We'll show both examples.

[00:10:40] Jonas: Is it possible to provision ephemeral pre-warmed capacity that only runs during scheduled reports - like cron-driven prewarm?
[10:52] Luis: Yes, you can configure scheduled warm windows where nodes are prewarmed and ready. That's a common pattern for nightly report spikes.

[00:11:05] Priya: A bit about observability: we need per-route token cost breakdown and traces tied to customer id. How deep is the Console?
[11:20] Casey: Console gives token-level cost, per-route latency histograms, model-level breakdowns, and you can attach request metadata to trace across your services. We can export logs to your SIEM (Splunk/Datadog).
[11:33] Selena: We need audit logs shipped into our own S3 and immutable retention for 90 days.
[11:40] Maya: Supported — we'll include retention options in the security doc.

[00:11:55] Tom: Any limits on concurrency per GPU? What about batching settings?
[11:58] Luis: Concurrency and batching settings are tunable. We recommend continuous batching for throughput workloads and manual concurrency caps for latency-critical endpoints. The runtime picks kernels and batch sizes based on sequence length distribution.

[00:12:20] Priya: One of our employees mentioned they saw mention of "KV cash" in a doc — hope that's not a billing bug.
[12:30] Maya: (laugh) must be a transcript misread. We'll confirm all naming.

[00:12:45] Jonas: Ok let's stage the benchmark: we can provide a 7-day traffic dump. Can Redwood replay that against a reserved pool with our model? What access do you need?
[12:58] Luis: We'll need a sanitized trace or replay artifact (we can consume ndjson or a simple curl request list). For Private/on-prem we can run the benchmark in your environment; for hosted we can run replay in our lab with a forwarded dataset. We'll provide a step-by-step.

[00:13:20] Priya: For the benchmark, we want to test both latency-critical chat and long-form summarization. Can you run both?
[13:27] Luis: Yes, we'll run both scenarios and measure p50/p95/p99 and token throughput. We'll also capture cold-start behavior.

[00:13:40] Selena: What about isolation guarantees if we need to escalate to per-tenant GPUs — is that a separate procurement item?
[13:52] Casey: It's typically part of a larger Dedicated/Private engagement. We can design a topology with tenant-affined nodes; this usually increases baseline cost because utilization falls. We'll provide modelings for 2 options: shared reserved with fencing vs per-tenant dedicated.

[00:14:15] Maya: Quick recap of risks: cost if you size for worst-case long outputs; third-party fallback policy that could violate residency if misconfigured; and warm-pool sizing complexity. We can mitigate each with pricing options, enforced routing policies, and scheduled warm windows.

[00:14:40] Priya: Good. One more on encryption: we need end-to-end encryption at rest and KMS control for model artifacts. Does Redwood allow customer-managed model artifact keys?
[14:55] Luis: Yes in Private, model artifact keys can be customer-managed. For Hosted we offer envelope encryption with customer KMS for higher tiers.

[00:15:10] Tom: Procurement timeline — we want a proposal by next week if possible.
[15:18] Maya: We'll aim to get an initial pricing + architecture note by 2027-05-07.

[00:15:35] Selena: Any known limitations with very long context (4k-8k tokens)?
[15:48] Luis: Performance scales with context — KV cache size, memory constraints, and kernel choices matter. For 8k use cases we recommend larger GPU memory (e.g., H100/80GB variants) and quantized kernels where possible. We'll include a recommendation.

[00:16:10] Priya: Are there prebuilt integrations for our infra (we use GCP + Anthos in some zones)?
[16:22] Casey: We support cloud regions on GCP and Private can integrate with Anthos; network peering and IAM mapping are the typical integration points.

[00:16:40] Jonas: Any chance you can give a back-of-envelope for cost — say for keeping 8 GPUs reserved monthly vs using hosted burst for the same peak?
[16:55] Maya: We'll show a side-by-side. Hosted burst tends to be higher unit cost but no commitment. 8 committed GPUs multiply by cogs and infra overhead; we'll include an example that maps to your QPS.

[00:17:10] Tom: On SLA — what's the uptime SLA for Dedicated?
[17:18] Maya: We offer SLA-backed uptime for Dedicated customers and can include latency SLOs in enterprise contracts with penalties or credit. We'll draft an example.

[00:17:35] Priya: Ok that's all I had for now. Anything else from Redwood?
[17:40] Luis: We'll prepare the benchmark playbook and warm-pool sizing doc. Also a short checklist for Private on-prem readiness if you want that path.
[17:49] Maya: I'll follow up with pricing matrix and security pack.

[00:18:05] Tom: Next steps recap — pricing + architecture by 2027-05-07, Heterodyne shares 7-day trace and compliance list by 2027-05-07, Redwood sets up benchmark run week of 2027-05-17.
[18:18] Priya: Sounds good.

[00:18:30] (some chatter, meeting wraps up)

Notes on transcript quality: intermittent microphone drop at ~00:02:20 and a brief section with crosstalk at ~00:14:15. Minor mis-transcriptions ("KV cash" instead of KV cache) present.

End of transcript.
